overview: The Somali Republic formed in 1960 by joining territories formerly administered by Britain and Italy. Its later history includes military government, civil war and renewed federal institutions.

periods.title: Union and republican government
periods.summary: Two former colonial territories united in 1960.

periods.title: Military government
periods.summary: Siad Barre seized power in 1969 and was overthrown in 1991.

periods.title: War and transitional institutions
periods.summary: Civil war and reconciliation efforts preceded new federal institutions.

periods.title: Federal institutions and disputed sovereignty
periods.summary: Federal institutions developed while Somalia and Somaliland’s authorities disputed sovereignty.

items.text: On 1 July 1960, the former British Somaliland and the former Italian-administered territory united as the Somali Republic. A constitution followed in 1961. The imported outline represents that territorial framework; it does not establish who controlled every place in every later year.

Mohamed Siad Barre seized power in October 1969. His overthrow in 1991 was followed by civil war and repeated attempts to rebuild national government. These were changes in political authority, with devastating consequences for families and institutions.

The 2012 constitutional framework provided for a federal parliament with two chambers. The Upper House did not begin functioning until 2016, when states selected senators. Designing an institution on paper and making it work were separate stages.

Somaliland’s sovereignty remains disputed. Israel recognized it in December 2025, while Somalia objected and the African Union reaffirmed Somalia’s unity. The UN Security Council had reaffirmed Somalia’s sovereignty earlier that month. A single color on this map cannot resolve those competing positions.

sections.title: Learning to write and learning over the radio

items.text: In October 1972, the government adopted a modified Latin alphabet for Somali. Language specialists worked on textbooks, grammar and a dictionary. This was an important standardization of written Somali, rather than the invention of the Somali language.

A literacy campaign began in towns in 1973 and later spread to rural areas. Teachers, students, civil servants and members of the armed services taught after their regular work. Classrooms could depend on a whole community’s spare hours, not just a school timetable.

A published Somali writing sample is “Kacaanka Jira: Ama Muxuu Aadamuhu U Socdaa Isagoo Adhax Taagan”, paired with “The Upright Revolution: Or Why Humans Walk Upright”. Khaloudy Mohamed Sa’eed and Abdillahi Raage translated Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o’s story for Jalada in 2016. It shows the language in modern literary use.

The SOMDEL education programme, launched in 2001, combined radio lessons, printed materials and local tutorials. Lessons covered reading, arithmetic, health and livelihoods. Teachers could replay recordings where radio reception was poor: the classroom’s teacher could arrive on a cassette.

Halimo, a tailor in Hargeisa, began SOMDEL classes in 2004. She reported that literacy helped her measure cloth, keep accounts and record customers’ debts, while helping her children with homework. School skills could matter at the sewing table as well as in an examination.

sections.title: Milk, health and voices worth preserving

items.text: A study published in 2010 describes women’s networks carrying camel milk from mobile herders to Puntland’s towns. Men generally milked the camels in the studied households; women then decided how to allocate milk between children, other household needs and sale.

Collectors followed herds as they moved and traded milk for cash or household goods. Transporters carried it toward urban markets and brought supplies back. This was a carefully organized supply chain, even without a supermarket warehouse or refrigerated delivery van.

At Godod School in Mudug, a 2024 report describes a lesson on menstruation and reusable pads. Student Nafiso explained that buying pads could strain her family’s budget. Water, toilets, clear information and private facilities all helped students manage ordinary bodily needs while staying in class.

Radio Mogadishu’s archive holds roughly 45,000 audio tapes recording politics, language and cultural life. A 2026 preservation project addressed aging tapes and damage. A nation’s history can survive in recorded voices as well as stone monuments, but both need care.

ending.text: Somalia continues as a state, with federal institutions and unresolved territorial disputes. War and changes of government did not end Somali communities, language or cultural life.

sources.title: African Union UN Mission: Federal Republic of Somalia
sources.note: Official state profile, updated February 2026; formation of the republic on 1 July 1960 and 1961 constitution.

sources.title: Somali Upper House: Historical Background
sources.note: Institutional history: 1969 coup, 1991 collapse, transitional institutions, 2012 constitution and first functioning Senate in 2016. English has grammatical mistakes; do not copy its erroneous use of since for until.

sources.title: UN DPPA: Khaled Khiari’s Security Council briefing, 29 December 2025
sources.note: Full indexed official briefing checked; direct fetch failed. Records Israeli recognition on 26 December, Somali objection, AU position and Security Council affirmation of Somalia’s sovereignty. Do not treat a country representative’s statement as the UN’s own position.

sources.title: World Bank: Appraisal of a Third Education Project in the Somali Democratic Republic, 1977
sources.note: Report 1334-SO, 26 July 1977, Appendix II pages 1 to 2. Contemporary education appraisal; government literacy percentages are not independently established and are omitted.

sources.title: Jalada Africa: Kacaanka Jira, Somali translation, 2016
sources.note: Primary publication, 22 March 2016; exact title, Somali label, two translators and linked English counterpart. Modern translation of Ngũgĩ’s story, not an ancient Somali text.

sources.title: Michele Nori: The golden Udder, in Adding Value to Livestock Diversity
sources.note: LPP, LIFE Network, IUCN-WISP and FAO, 2010, printed pages 99 to 102; Puntland study based on projects in 2001 to 2007. Specific local evidence rather than a timeless rule for all Somalis.

sources.title: UNESCO Institute for Lifelong Learning: Somali Distance Education and Literacy
sources.note: 2014 programme assessment: radio lessons and named learner testimonies. Halimo’s Hargeisa home is in Somaliland; place is not used as a sovereignty claim.

sources.title: UNICEF Somalia: Menstrual management is not a secret
sources.note: 2 April 2024 report, Godod School in Mudug, PMWDO lessons, Nafiso’s experience and school water/sanitation services.

sources.title: UNESCO: Protecting Somalia’s documentary heritage
sources.note: 22 June 2026 account of preservation workshop and Radio Mogadishu’s approximately 45,000 tapes. Archive evidence only; the article’s compressed campaign chronology is not used.
